transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood CSM), Jordan, Priya, Liam, Anika (CrestEdge)

Summary:
Quick sync on results from last week's microburst/TTFT experiments, discuss kernel tradeoffs for streaming first token, sequence length tuning, and agreement on next steps for a 3-hour soak and security follow-up. Some noisy audio; a couple names fuzzy in the transcription.

Topics:
- TTFT regressions observed on the 08/14 cluster patch
- Streaming handshake latency and early-byte path
- Sequence length distribution and KV cache sizing
- Kernel choices (fast-gemm vs attention-chunk) and quantization impact
- Rollout plan for canary + soak

Action items (recorded in notes above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Okay folks, hi thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Evan and I from Redwood, Samira on the CSM side. CrestEdge team?
[00:07] Jordan: Yeah Jordan here. Priya is on, Liam and Anika as well.
[00:12] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda: results recap, kernel tuning, seqlen, and canary plan. Evan you wanna kick off with the numbers?
[00:20] Evan (SE): Sure. So we re-ran the fastpath with the attention-chunk change and the microburst hedging enabled. Baseline before the change — median TTFT around 220ms, 95th at 620ms. After patch we saw median drop to ~135ms, 95th to ~370ms on the synthetic load, but real traffic shows a tail at ~480ms when bursts align. There's some jitter in the KV cache hits, we saw hit-rate down to 68% on one run which amplified tail.
[01:02] Priya: Sorry can you repeat the 95th numbers? They— I missed the first one.
[01:06] Evan (SE): Yeah baseline 95th ~620ms, patched 95th ~370ms synthetic, but on production-like traces we still measure ~480ms tail depending on seqlen distribution.
[01:18] Jordan: That 68% KV hit— is that because the cache size was too small or because request prefixes are more diverse?
[01:24] Evan (SE): Good question. It looks like two factors: prefix diversity and some requests with longer effective context that push older keys out. We also noticed our default KV shard sizing put hot prefixes across nodes causing extra cross-shard lookups.
[01:38] Anika (SRE): On our side we saw spiky cross-node latency spikes when big seq requests hit.
[01:42] Evan (SE): Right. One mitigation is increasing per-worker KV capacity and switching to sticky routing for hot prefixes, but that increases memory footprint. Another is a small sequence-length clamp for streaming first-byte path to reduce cache churn.
[01:55] Maya (AE): Can you explain the clamp tradeoff in plain terms?
[01:58] Evan (SE): Sure — for the early-response fastpath we can cap the effective seqlen we consider for KV caching to, say, 512 tokens even if the client sends 1024. That reduces cache pressure and improves TTFT for most requests, but long-context queries will get slightly degraded rerun cost or fall back to the slower path which increases end-to-end for those rare requests. It's a latency v cost/accuracy tradeoff.
[02:25] Priya: If we clamp at 512, what percent of our traffic would be affected? I can share distribution but off the top — maybe 7–9% over 512.
[02:32] Maya (AE): Helpful. Priya can you upload the seqlen percentiles after the call? Evan will use that to recommend clamp threshold.
[02:40] Liam (CTO): Also curious: the attention-chunk kernel — is that something you'll ship in hosted immediately or do we need dedicated?
[02:48] Evan (SE): We can push it to hosted experimental instances but for guaranteed SLOs we'd recommend a dedicated pool for the pilot end-state. The kernel change touches some assembly-fast paths and needs a more conservative rollout on shared infra.
[02:58] Jordan: Is there a measurable accuracy difference with attention-chunk vs fast-gemm?
[03:03] Evan (SE): In our evals we saw no deterministic output deltas for float32 but quantized INT4/INT8 paths show tiny token-level diffs — within acceptable ranges for most assistant workloads. If your use-case is low hallucination tolerance, we should run the prompt set through both kernels.
[03:20] Priya: Okay we'll need that prompt set run.
[03:23] Maya (AE): We'll run Redwood's eval harness and share the CSV.
[03:27] Samira (CSM): Quick note — CrestEdge had asked about SOC2 scope and audit logs earlier, do we need to align that with the dedicated ask?
[03:35] Liam: Yes, dedicated helpful for our compliance team. We also need KMS integration for payload encryption at rest.
[03:42] Maya (AE): Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated; we'll attach the security docs.
[03:47] Jordan: Thank you. Back to microburst— what about hedging parameters? You mentioned microburst hedging earlier.
[03:53] Evan (SE): Right— we enabled a 20ms early-hedge for the streaming handshake which reduces first-byte variance. It gives a small extra compute cost for hedged requests but drops the 99th by ~120ms in our tests. The cost/benefit depends on your SLOs.
[04:12] Anika (SRE): Does hedging interact with batching? We batch at the runtime layer, right?
[04:16] Evan (SE): Yes, continuous batching is in play. Hedging is coordinated with the router; when a request exceeds the hedge threshold without response we issue a hedged request to a warm path. It can increase token-level compute due to duplicate work but we have de-dup caches for final outputs.
[04:33] Priya: Any impact on KV cache coherence with hedged duplicates?
[04:36] Evan (SE): Minimal — hedged requests typically hit the same KV version. If they diverge we have a reconciliation path but shouldn't be common.
[04:42] Jordan: Can you walk through the proposed canary/soak plan?
[04:46] Evan (SE): Sure. Proposed: 1) push attention-chunk + hedging to a canary dedicated pool (10% traffic) for 24 hours, 2) run a 3-hour soak at 100% with synthetic blended load capturing your seqlen histogram, 3) if soak passes 95th/T target we roll to 50% then full. We'll also run the evals in parallel to check output diffs.
[05:07] Priya: For the 3-hour soak, do we need a separate host or can we do it in hosted?
[05:11] Evan (SE): Dedicated is safer because of kernel variability. Hosted experimental may be acceptable for an initial smoke, but for soak we recommend dedicated reserved nodes.
[05:19] Maya (AE): Cost implications— we'll include a reserved 6-week trial pricing and delta vs hosted in the doc.
[05:25] Liam: For auditing, can we capture token-level latency traces? Our compliance team will want per-token histograms.
[05:31] Samira (CSM): Yes, we can enable per-token tracing for the pilot with retention limited to the trial. We'll coordinate retention window.
[05:39] Jordan: One weird data point: on 08/16 we saw an odd bump in TTFT correlating with a model version change — could model params be affecting kernel performance?
[05:47] Evan (SE): Model topology can change memory layout and kernel coverage; a model with different attention bias or more heads can change kernel heuristics. We track model build tags and recommend pinning a model artifact for the soak.
[05:58] Priya: We'll pin to the v2026-07-30 artifact used in the synthetic runs.
[06:02] Evan (SE): Great. Also we have a small optimization: switching the matmul path to fast-gemm on layers 1..6 only, leaving later layers on attention-chunk, that hybrid approach reduced CPU-to-GPU memcpy overhead in our internal tests and trimmed ~10–15ms from median.
[06:22] Anika (SRE): That sounds promising but is it stable?
[06:25] Evan (SE): It's been stable in infra tests but we still want soak runs.
[06:29] Jordan: Any changes to model quantization planned? We saw INT8 gave 2x speed but some odd token probability shifts on our LLM.
[06:37] Evan (SE): Quantization is a big lever. INT8/INT4 can change logits and downstream behavior. For this pilot we recommend keeping float32 for safety and run quant evals separately. If you accept small output variance we can explore INT8 on a narrow set.
[06:53] Maya (AE): Ok the plan then — dedicate a canary pool, run 24h canary then 3h soak, eval outputs, and if passes proceed roll. Priya to share request histograms, Evan to push kernel, Maya to send cost + SLO docs. Samira to set up security artifact share.
[07:11] Priya: I'll send the histogram and a sanitized sample of requests by tomorrow.
[07:15] Evan (SE): I'll push the attention-chunk build to the test cluster by Friday and attach a simple runbook.
[07:21] Maya (AE): We'll also include a short runbook for sticky routing and KV shard sizing changes.
[07:25] Liam: How do we revert if we see tail regressions in canary?
[07:29] Evan (SE): Instant rollback to the previous kernel + routing config. We keep canary traffic split and route a small % to fallback. Also we have automatic fallback rules if 95th exceeds threshold for 15 minutes.
[07:41] Jordan: Good. A couple of quick clarifying questions — do you have a recommended hedging threshold for our workload?
[07:47] Evan (SE): Given your seqlen mix, I'd start with a 20ms hedge and iterate to 10ms if compute cost too high; we'll measure 99th reduction and delta cost.
[07:58] Priya: About KV memory footprint: what's the estimated increase if we double per-worker KV capacity?
[08:03] Evan (SE): Ballpark +18–22% RAM per worker depending on sharding config. We'll provide exact numbers after we see your histogram.
[08:12] Anika (SRE): Any network implications for sticky routing? More cross-zone affinity?
[08:17] Evan (SE): It can increase intra-cluster affinity and reduce some cross-node traffic; overall network should be neutral or slightly improved because we avoid cross-shard lookups.
[08:26] Maya (AE): Samira, do we have the security doc link handy?
[08:29] Samira (CSM): Yes — I'll paste it in the follow-up email; it's the SOC2 + KMS integration doc.
[08:34] Jordan: One more: can Redwood produce a short CSV of run metrics we can ingest into our internal dashboard?
[08:39] Evan (SE): Yep we can provide per-request latency CSV with token-level times and kernel tag, anonymized.
[08:45] Priya: That will help our SRE to correlate spikes.
[08:49] Maya (AE): Great. Any other concerns from CrestEdge?
[08:53] Liam: No, sounds like a solid plan. We'll expect the docs and the kernel by EOD Friday.
[08:59] Maya (AE): Perfect — Samira will own the calendar invite for the canary kickoff; target Monday 2026-08-23 for canary push.
[09:07] Samira (CSM): I'll send invites and the security artifact link.
[09:10] Jordan: Thanks everyone.
[09:12] Priya: Thanks.
[09:14] (transcription noise, overlapping voices)
[09:20] End of recording.
